article.title: From Daryl Gates to Digital Surveillance: Is Los Angeles Really Protecting Immigrants?
article.author: Sharon Kyle
article.content: The opinions expressed here are solely the author's and do not reflect the opinions or beliefs of the LA Progressive. In the 2026 Los Angeles mayoral race, City Councilmember Nithya Raman has accused Mayor Karen Bass of failing to adequately protect immigrant communities from federal immigration enforcement. That is a serious charge. It deserves serious examination. But Raman's criticism has raised another question, one that connects directly to Los Angeles's history of policing. During a mayoral debate, Raman invoked the LAPD's 1979 Special Order 40 as a model of immigrant protection, describing the policy associated with the Daryl Gates era as a “gold standard.” She subsequently clarified that she was praising the policy, not Gates himself. That distinction matters. So does the extraordinary difference between the world of 1979 and the world of 2026. If we are going to evaluate which candidate can best protect immigrant communities, we must look beyond historical comparisons and political accusations. We must examine how government power operates today—and whether our leaders understand the technological capabilities of the institutions they oversee. What Special Order 40 Actually Did Special Order 40 was adopted in 1979, during Mayor Tom Bradley's administration, when Daryl Gates was chief of the LAPD. It prohibited officers from initiating police action solely to determine someone's immigration status. The purpose was important. Immigrant residents needed confidence that reporting crimes or cooperating with police would not automatically expose them to immigration enforcement. But Special Order 40 was not an absolute prohibition on cooperation with federal immigration authorities. Nor did it eliminate the broader problems associated with policing under Gates. As discussed in Part 1 , Gates presided over an era marked by aggressive policing, Operation Hammer, and profound mistrust between the LAPD and Black communities. A policy offering meaningful protections to immigrants could coexist with practices that inflicted serious harm on other populations. That contradiction deserves recognition. But there is another problem with treating Special Order 40 as a contemporary standard. It was developed for a world in which the collection, storage, and exchange of personal information were far more limited. Technology has fundamentally changed what cooperation between government agencies can mean. The Difference Between 1979 and 2026 In 1979, police generally gathered information about someone's identity or movements through direct encounters, investigations, and comparatively limited record systems. Today, government agencies can collect, retain, search, and exchange enormous quantities of information. Automated license plate readers record vehicle movements. Booking fingerprints can enter national databases accessible to multiple agencies. Commercial databases can assemble information about people's addresses, associations, and activities. Information collected for one purpose can become useful for another. An LAPD officer does not necessarily have to question someone about immigration status—or personally contact an ICE agent—for information collected through local policing to become accessible to federal authorities. That does not mean every database connection constitutes an unlawful disclosure. It means effective immigrant protection requires more than restrictions on individual officers' conduct. A city can comply with an older policy while leaving residents exposed to dangers its authors could scarcely have imagined. That is why I find Raman's invocation of Special Order 40 as a contemporary “gold standard” inadequate. The question is whether Los Angeles's protections have kept pace with the institutions they are intended to restrain. The Surveillance Warnings Los Angeles Has Already Received These concerns are not speculative. For years, the ACLU of Southern California and the Stop LAPD Spying Coalition have documented and challenged the LAPD's expanding surveillance capabilities. In litigation reported in 2017, the ACLU and Electronic Frontier Foundation documented that the LAPD and Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department were collecting approximately three million license plate scans weekly and had accumulated roughly half a billion records. Those historical figures reveal the extraordinary scale surveillance had already reached nearly a decade ago. The records concerned ordinary motorists, not simply people suspected of crimes. Such databases can reveal where people travel, worship, seek medical treatment, or participate in political activity. Stop LAPD Spying has examined what it calls the architecture of surveillance : the interconnected technologies, databases, agencies, and institutional relationships through which police gather and use information. Its research has connected data-driven policing to racialized enforcement and the displacement of marginalized communities. In its report Automating Banishment , the coalition examines relationships among policing, surveillance, real estate development, and the regulation of urban space. The coalition has also raised concerns about real-time crime centers, automated license plate readers, and private surveillance vendors. Not every allegation made by advocates has been conclusively established. Nor does every surveillance technology necessarily violate the law. But Los Angeles has received detailed warnings about these capabilities for years. That history creates responsibilities for elected officials. When evaluating Bass, we should ask what her administration has done to investigate these concerns, independently assess surveillance systems, and ensure compliance with city protections. When evaluating Raman, we should ask whether her proposals address the broader surveillance infrastructure or only particular relationships with federal immigration authorities. Both candidates should explain what they would do when a surveillance technology cannot be adequately controlled. Would they restrict it, suspend it, or end the city's use of it? Raman's Criticism of Bass Deserves Scrutiny Raman has accused the Bass administration of allowing LAPD practices that potentially expose immigrants to federal enforcement. She has raised concerns about information sharing and questioned whether the city has done enough to prevent cooperation with ICE. Those concerns deserve examination. But political accountability requires factual precision. Reporting has raised questions about LAPD booking fingerprints entering national systems accessible to immigration authorities. That is troubling, particularly if information collected during routine policing can later facilitate immigration enforcement. But federal access to information does not, by itself, establish that LAPD officials deliberately transmitted it to ICE in violation of city policy. Similarly, concerns about automated license plate readers require examining who controls the information, who can access it, how long it is retained, and whether vendors or other agencies can disclose it. The LAPD has said it found no evidence that its license plate reader information was shared with immigration enforcement agencies. That assertion deserves independent verification. It should neither be accepted uncritically nor disregarded without contrary evidence. Raman is entitled to challenge Bass. Holding an incumbent mayor accountable for the police department is precisely what a challenger should do. But which practices does Raman believe violate sanctuary protections? What evidence supports those allegations? What corrective measures would she implement? Bass must answer equally specific questions. Has her administration independently audited information-sharing systems? Has it examined vulnerabilities created by technology vendors? How does it verify compliance? What consequences follow violations? These questions matter more than competing claims about historical commitment. What Los Angeles Has Actually Done Los Angeles has not been standing still. In 2023, Councilmembers Raman, Eunisses Hernandez, and Hugo Soto-Martínez introduced a motion directing the city to develop stronger sanctuary protections. Following Donald Trump's reelection in November 2024, Bass worked with City Attorney Hydee Feldstein Soto to accelerate the legislation. The City Council adopted the ordinance, and Bass signed it into law in December 2024. The ordinance restricted the use of city personnel, property, resources, and information to support federal immigration enforcement, subject to legal exceptions. In July 2025, Bass issued Executive Directive No. 12, instructing city departments to reinforce those protections. Both Raman and Bass deserve recognition for their contributions. Raman helped initiate the legislative effort. Bass helped accelerate its completion, signed the ordinance, and subsequently directed its implementation. But adopting protections and ensuring their effectiveness are different responsibilities. The mayor oversees city departments, appoints leadership, and influences enforcement priorities. The City Council also exercises legislative, budgetary, and oversight authority. Neither candidate can reasonably claim that immigrant protection is solely the other's responsibility. And neither should be judged solely by legislation supported or directives issued. The question is whether those measures work. A sanctuary designation cannot substitute for effective administration, meaningful oversight, and adequate resources. The Foothold: When Surveillance Expands Beyond Its Original Targets This is where my Foothold Theory becomes relevant. The theory begins with a proposition: Those seeking to accumulate power often find their easiest opportunities among populations least able to resist. They are the low-hanging fruit. Immigrants facing detention or deportation may have limited ability to challenge government practices. Public officials can justify extraordinary measures by portraying targeted populations as dangerous, undeserving, or outside the circle of people whose rights merit protection. When the public accepts those justifications, those exercising power may gain more than an immediate advantage. They gain a foothold. In surveillance, that foothold may take the form of databases, expanded monitoring capabilities, information-sharing arrangements, or weakened expectations of privacy. Once established, those systems need not remain confined to the populations originally used to justify them. A system capable of tracking an immigrant's movements can track a citizen's movements. A database revealing where one vulnerable population lives, works, or travels can reveal the same information about others. And a surveillance capability created under one administration can be inherited by another with different priorities and fewer restraints. This does not mean every official supporting surveillance intends to abuse it. But it would be dangerous to assume that the first population subjected to an intrusive government practice will necessarily be the last. That is the difference between examining surveillance as a collection of technologies and examining it as an accumulation of institutional power. What the Miner's Canary Is Telling Us In Part 2, I described the disappearance of Black Los Angeles through the metaphor of the Miner's Canary. When the canary began to suffer, miners knew the air had become dangerous. The warning was not simply about the bird. It was about conditions threatening everyone. Immigrant communities may now be revealing another danger. When government can monitor movements, assemble personal information, and connect databases across agencies, those capabilities create risks extending beyond immigration enforcement. The Miner's Canary identifies the warning. My Foothold Theory asks who is accumulating power, how they are doing it, and what prevents them from expanding its use. Together, these ideas explain why defending vulnerable populations is not merely an act of compassion. It is also an act of collective self-preservation. Martin Luther King Jr. warned that “injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.” I understand that warning not only as a moral principle but as a practical observation about power. Those willing to exploit one population's vulnerability have not necessarily demonstrated that they will respect the rights of others when circumstances change. Why should we assume they will stop? What a Mayor Must Understand The debate over immigration enforcement returns us to the central question running through this series. What understanding should we require of someone seeking to serve as mayor of Los Angeles? The mayor cannot control federal immigration law or prevent every federal enforcement action. But the mayor can direct city departments, appoint leadership, propose budgets, oversee compliance, and work with the City Council to strengthen safeguards. Those responsibilities require more than good intentions. They require understanding how modern institutions accumulate information, how technology expands their capabilities, and how authority granted for one purpose can be used for another. Raman is right to demand accountability from Bass. But invoking a policy adopted in 1979 does not establish what protections are adequate in 2026. Bass is right to point to the city's sanctuary commitments. But issuing directives does not establish that those protections are effective in practice. Both candidates must explain how they would identify and close gaps between policy and enforcement. Both must demonstrate an understanding of the technological realities confronting immigrant communities. And both must recognize that inadequate safeguards threaten more than those currently targeted by immigration enforcement. The measure of leadership is not merely whether a mayor supports immigrant rights in principle. It is whether the mayor understands the powers threatening those rights and can use the authority of the office to restrain them. The Danger of Failing to Recognize Power Los Angeles's history offers an important lesson. Government power can expand through policies, practices, and technologies that initially appear limited in purpose. The most vulnerable may experience the consequences first. But they are not necessarily the last. This is why historical ignorance is dangerous in political leadership. A mayor who does not understand how institutions acquire and exercise power may fail to recognize new threats until they are deeply embedded. A mayor who disregards vulnerable communities may overlook the warnings those communities provide. And a public that assumes those warnings concern only immigrants, Black residents, or other marginalized populations may discover too late that the protections it neglected were protections everyone needed. The question confronting Los Angeles is not whether Special Order 40 was progressive in 1979. It was. The question is whether our leaders understand what it takes to protect people in 2026. If Los Angeles cannot prevent powerful institutions from using modern surveillance systems against its most vulnerable residents, what assurance do the rest of us have that those systems will not eventually be used against us? That is the question both candidates should be required to answer. Part 3 of the four-part series “Who Gets to Lead Los Angeles? History, Race, Immigration, and Political Responsibility.” Part 4 examines how U.S. foreign and economic policies have contributed to migration, and what responsibility American leaders bear for the consequences.
